source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality, Table 2
finding: Table 2 now checked. Take The Best, weighted tallying, regression and tallying are tied in accuracy on the German cities task. The two linear models that use all cues with both signs are clearly lower. The authors say the gap comes from the recognition principle being built into tallying and TTB, not from weighting.
numbers: 83 German cities (>100,000 inhabitants), 9 ecological cues plus recognition, simulated individuals, 500 simulations per cell. Average proportion correct over 10/20/50/75/100% of cue values known: TTB .621/.635/.663/.678/.691, average .658. Weighted tallying average .658. Regression .625/.635/.657/.674/.694, average .657. Tallying .656. Weighted linear model .623. Unit-weight linear model .621. Minimalist .647. Take The Last .645.
quote: the Take The Best algorithm drew as many correct inferences as any of the other algorithms, and more than some.
limits: Regression was given all city populations and refit per simulated person (in-sample, 'more information than was given to any of the competitors'), so it is not a cross-validated competitor. One environment, one criterion, simulated knowledge states. Differences among the top four are 0.1-0.2 points. Later work (a18) finds regression slightly ahead on 63 data sets.
agent_relevance: Corrects the earlier unverified a02/a03 quote. The honest headline is 'ties with regression at lower search cost', not 'beats optimal'. Cite .658 versus .657, never a margin.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way, speed section and less-is-more result
finding: TTB looked up far fewer cue values than the integration algorithms, which always look up everything. The less-is-more effect shows up in the same simulation: accuracy peaks near 77% when about two thirds of the cities are recognized and falls when more are known.
numbers: TTB searched between 2 (recognition values only) and 20 cue values (9 cues plus recognition for two cities). Peak around 77% correct at partial recognition. The text for the half-recognized case was cut in the copy, so that average is not recorded.
limits: Frugality is counted in cue lookups from memory, not seconds or tokens. A later study found TTB is not always faster in people (K19).
agent_relevance: Frugality metric for our agent must be tokens or checks run, measured per item; the paper's unit is cue lookups.

source: Glockner & Broder (2011) Processing of recognition information and additional cues: a model-based analysis of choice, confidence, and response time. Judgment and Decision Making 6(1), 23-42
finding: Re-checked against the full PDF. When cue values of unrecognized cities are also shown, most people are best described by a compensatory parallel constraint satisfaction model, not by recognition heuristic or take-the-best. The 77.5% figure is confirmed.
numbers: 120 paired comparisons of US cities with 3 cues plus recognition; 3 subjects not classified so N = 80. Classification (MM-ML, choice + time + confidence): RHe 4, TTB 12 (15.0%), RHe/TTB 2, PCS1 38, PCS2 24 (PCS total 62 = 77.5%). Mean choice-deviation p(error): TTB .16, RHe .28, PCS1 .19, PCS2 .14. PCS1 versus RHe and TTB only: 73% PCS users.
quote: For 77.5% of the subjects, overall behavior was best explained by a compensatory parallel constraint satisfaction (PCS) strategy.
limits: Cues were shown on screen, not retrieved from memory; the authors say memory-based tasks may favor TTB (Broder & Schiffer found more TTB-consistent choices there). Classification depends on the model set chosen. One city-size domain.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, cues are shown in the prompt, which is the condition where people mostly integrate. This argues against assuming a stop-at-first-cue prompt is natural; it must be tested.

source: Glockner & Broder (2011), process fit of strategy users (Table 4)
finding: Even people classified as TTB or RHe users did not show the decision times and confidence the strategy predicts. Their classification came from choices alone.
numbers: Share of classified users whose time contrasts were significant: RHe 0, TTB .25, PCS1 .61, PCS2 .71. Confidence contrasts significant: RHe .25, TTB .50, PCS1 .82, PCS2 .75. Median correlation of predicted and observed time: RHe .02, TTB .05, PCS1 .20, PCS2 .11.
limits: Time and confidence predictions for TTB depend on auxiliary process assumptions. Small N per class (12 TTB users).
agent_relevance: Same outputs can come from different processes. For the agent, log which checks were actually run, not only the final answer, before calling a rule 'TTB-like'.

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making. American Psychologist 34(7), 571-582
finding: Opened and read. Linear models with arbitrary or equal weights (right signs, standardized variables) predict nearly as well as fitted weights and beat human judges in the studies reviewed (via Dawes & Corrigan 1974). Equal weights beat randomly weighted models on average, which Dawes shows follows mathematically.
numbers: Table 1 columns are garbled in the text extraction, so only the pattern is quoted: equal-weight validity is at or above average random-weight validity in every example and close to cross-validated regression. Libby loan-officer example: officers classified 74% of 60 firms correctly, their linear models 72%, proper linear models about 78% on cross-validation, and the single ratio of assets to liabilities 80% (48 of 60).
quote: the whole trick is to know what variables to look at and then know how to add.
limits: Review of 1970s studies; predictors with known direction and positive intercorrelation. Dawes warns that unit weights on unstandardized variables are meaningless. Numeric prediction, not LLM answers.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'never opened' flag on Dawes. Supports equal-weight vote or checklist counts when the sign of each check is known in advance and data are few.

source: Griffin et al. (2026) Random Rule Forest: interpretable ensembles of LLM-generated questions (v3)
finding: The only LLM study found that uses a plain unit-weight vote (a tallying rule) and compares it with learned weights on the same features. An LLM writes yes/no questions; the answers are counted against one threshold. On two low-base-rate tasks it matched or beat elastic-net logistic regression and zero/few-shot prompting.
numbers: Startup founders (positives <2%, Npos = 158): RRF precision .109, recall .082, F0.5 .102 (+-.015) versus elastic-net LogReg F0.5 .080, engineered ML .086, embeddings+XGBoost .069, best prompting baseline o3 few-shot .088. Differences not statistically separable (founder-level bootstrap). Phase I trials (prevalence .553): RRF PR-AUC .638, ROC-AUC .596, F1 .655 versus LogReg PR-AUC .632, ROC-AUC .594, F1 .641; HINT has best F1 .665.
limits: Authors' own framework; margins are small. They claim no founder-level win and no discrimination advantage; the gain is in F0.5 at an operating point. 10 repeats of 10-fold nested CV; prompting baselines run once.
agent_relevance: Direct Dawes analogue for LLM checks: a count of passed yes/no checks is a competitive default when data for fitting weights are scarce.

source: Griffin et al. (2026) Random Rule Forest, Appendix I (unit-weight vote versus learned weights, positive-count mechanism)
finding: The unit-weight vote's advantage over learned weights shrinks as the number of positive training examples grows, with a knee near 100 positives. This is a bias-variance crossover for an LLM-feature pipeline. It tracks the count of positives, not the class ratio.
numbers: Pre-registered subsampling sweep. F0.5 gap (vote minus elastic net) vs Npos: Spearman rho = -0.50 (p = 1.8e-6) for founders, -0.38 (p = 1.1e-4) for clinical trials. Knee near Npos about 100. Holding Npos = 158 and raising prevalence above about 5% turns the gap slightly negative (elastic net ahead). At the founder operating point the gap is +0.010.
limits: One feature pipeline, two domains, F0.5 only; no PR-AUC advantage. Positive count, not total cases, is the unit, which matters for rare outcomes.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the crossover between a learned weighting and plain counting sits near 100 positive cases here, which fits Parpart's 20-100 range for house prices. Our S0 class record should expect on the order of 100 labelled cases before fitted weights pay off.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park & Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction rivals human crowd accuracy
finding: An unweighted aggregate (median per question across 12 LLMs) matched a human crowd of 925 on 31 binary forecasting questions. The crowd was not better than its best member, so equal weighting gave no gain over picking the best single model.
numbers: LLM crowd mean Brier .20 (SD .12) vs human crowd .19 (SD .19), t(60) = 0.19, p = .85. Single models: GPT-4 .15, GPT-4 with Bing .16, Bard .19, Falcon-180B .21, Claude 2 .21, Llama-2-70B .25, Coral .38. A no-information forecast scores .25. Study 2: giving GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median improved accuracy 17-28%.
limits: 2023-2024 models, 31 questions, one tournament. No comparison with fitted weights. GPT-4 alone beat the crowd, so this supports equal-weight pooling as safe, not as better.
agent_relevance: Partial support for equal-weight pooling across models, with a warning: with a clearly stronger member, weight-free pooling can lose to that member. Gap 8 stays open for same-model samples.

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When not to trust language models: effectiveness of parametric and non-parametric memories (PopQA). ACL 2023
finding: Subject-entity popularity (Wikipedia page views) predicts whether an LLM answers a factual question correctly. This is an LLM version of recognition validity. A popularity threshold used as a cheap routing rule (retrieve only for unpopular entities) beat always retrieving.
numbers: PopQA 14k questions on long-tail entities. Correlation of log-popularity and accuracy about 0.4 for GPT-3 davinci-003, about 0.1 for GPT-Neo 1.3B. Scaling mostly helps above log10 popularity 4. Adaptive retrieval: up to 10% gain on PopQA; GPT-3 with GenRead+Contriever reached 46.5%, 5.3 points above any non-adaptive method; davinci-003 retrieved for only 40% of questions with BM25.
limits: Closed-book QA with 2022 models. Popularity is an external proxy, not the model's own sense of recognition. Threshold tuned per relation type on a dev set. Not a paired-comparison test of the recognition heuristic.
agent_relevance: Gap 5, first half: the cue 'entity is well known' has measurable validity for LLMs and the link strengthens with scale. Whether answers follow familiarity when other cues disagree is untested.

source: Ferrando, Obeso, Rajamanoharan & Nanda (2025) Do I know this entity? Knowledge awareness and hallucinations in language models. ICLR 2025
finding: Sparse-autoencoder directions in the model detect whether an entity is known. They act as an internal recognition cue and are causal: steering them makes the chat model refuse questions about known entities or hallucinate about unknown ones.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; no headline percentage recorded.
limits: Entity-attribute questions only. Shows the existence and causal role of a recognition signal, not its use in comparisons against other cues.
agent_relevance: A recognition signal exists inside the model and drives refusing versus answering. A known/unknown gate could be read from model behavior, but this paper does not test a stop-at-recognition rule.

source: Dies, Maynard, Savcisens & Eliassi-Rad (2026) Epistemic familiarity is associated with belief stability in LLMs (P-StaT)
finding: Across 21 LLMs, perturbations of unfamiliar synthetic statements shake model beliefs more than perturbations of familiar fictional ones. Familiarity is estimated from next-token probability of the object. It shows familiarity changes model behavior, not that models use it as a cue.
numbers: 21 LLMs, 3 domains. Behavioral belief retraction rates frequently exceed 0.5 for unfamiliar synthetic perturbations (abstract).
limits: Indirect. Stability under reframing, not paired-choice accuracy. Per-model numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Weak support that familiarity matters inside models. Gap 5 stays open: no study pits familiarity against contradicting cues.

source: Wang et al. (2025) When to reason: semantic router for vLLM (NeurIPS 2025 MLForSys workshop)
finding: A fine-tuned ModernBERT intent classifier routes each query to reasoning or non-reasoning mode. On MMLU-Pro with Qwen3-30B-A3B the router had higher accuracy and about half the tokens of the direct-inference baseline. Gains were largest in knowledge-heavy domains.
numbers: MMLU-Pro, 14 domains, Qwen3-30B-A3B on vLLM 0.10.1. Router 58.57% accuracy, 887.5 tokens, 13.09 s. Direct vLLM 48.33%, 1,722.1 tokens, 24.76 s. +10.24 points (p < .01), -48.5% tokens, -47.1% latency. Better in 11 of 14 domains; mixed in math and biology.
limits: Workshop paper, one model. The mode of the 'direct vLLM' headline row is unclear (six execution modes run), so the gain may reflect a weak default. Router classification accuracy itself not reported in the part read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a cheap classifier can route at lower tokens, but with an unclear baseline and no routing-accuracy figure it cannot fix the accuracy a router needs.

source: Kassenaar, Yang & Francois-Lavet (2026) Learning when to think: adaptive reasoning for test-time compute allocation
finding: One 1.5B distilled model learns to choose NoThink, Short or Long as its first token. The learned routing keeps accuracy near the base and cuts tokens; fixed brief modes lose accuracy. Routing sorts by difficulty and saves most where items are easy.
numbers: MATH-500 (3 seeds): free routing .78 at 2,811 tokens; base .79 at 4,796; Long-only .80 at 4,507; Short-only .72 at 2,030; NoThink-only .66 at 1,096. GSM8K: 76% fewer tokens than base, 44% fewer than the frontier at equal accuracy. AIME: matches the frontier, 12% shorter than base.
limits: One 1.5B model, math only, 3 seeds; routing is learned by RL, not a cheap external test. A two-mode router collapsed to one mode on Countdown, where difficulty is uniform.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: routing gains exist and track the spread of item difficulty. Homogeneous items give a router nothing to learn. NoThink-only costs 12 points on MATH-500, so a wrong route is expensive.

source: Tsvilodub, Huth, Franke, Deiseroth & Kauf (2026) Rewarding efficient reasoning improves abstention on underspecified tasks in reasoning models
finding: Independent lab, different method: reasoning models write chains of thought at least as long on unanswerable as on answerable matched items, while humans do not. A reward favoring efficient reasoning about answerability raised abstention and shortened chains.
numbers: Seven reasoning models (Qwen3-4B/32B, Olmo-3.1-32B, Falcon-H1-7B, Phi-4-mini, R1-Distill-Llama-8B and others) on QuestBench and AbstentionBench. Abstention accuracy credibly below answering accuracy (beta = 0.96 [0.87, 1.06]) and below humans (1.03 [0.73, 1.35]). Gap larger in reasoning than instruct models (beta = 1.67 [1.54, 1.80]). Fine-tuned 4B/8B models: +14.7% abstention on average, 44% shorter CoTs.
limits: Small open-weight models; human study exploratory. Items are underspecified, not Knightian. No frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly replicates in direction: another lab, matched item pairs, same cost of long chains on unanswerable items. The 17.3-point Bogdan figure itself is not replicated.

source: Fan, Li, Sun & Zhou (2025) Missing premise exacerbates overthinking: are reasoning models losing critical thinking skill?
finding: Reasoning models produce much longer responses and rarely abstain on ill-posed questions with a missing premise. Non-reasoning models give short answers that spot the problem, and their lengths on well-posed and ill-posed questions are similar.
numbers: Four curated MiP datasets (rule-based formulas, SWAMP, GSM8K and MATH variants). Models include o1, o1-mini, o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B, S1.1-32B and non-reasoning GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. One readable table row: QwQ-32B MiP-Formula 453 tokens, 20% abstain. Other per-model rates not reliably extracted (table garbled).
limits: Per-model numbers not cleanly extracted. Early-2025 models. Preprint under review at the time.
agent_relevance: Second independent lab for the direction of Gap 4. Frontier 2026 models and Knightian (not missing-premise) items remain untested.

source: Dekoninck, Baader & Vechev (2025) A unified approach to routing and cascading for LLMs (ICML 2025)
finding: Proves the optimal cascade rule and shows that the quality estimator decides whether routing or cascading pays. The combined cascade-routing method beats both on RouterBench.
numbers: Up to 8% improvement for cascading and up to 12% for routing over previous methods, measured against a linear-interpolation baseline on the cost-quality curve. Cascade routing beats both.
limits: Gains depend on a good quality estimator; where none exists, gains shrink. Not a replication of FrugalGPT's 98% cost claim.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 9: a stop-at-sufficient rule works only if the sufficiency signal is accurate. Routing accuracy is the whole game.

source: Yue et al. (2024) LLM cascades with mixture of thought representations for cost-efficient reasoning (ICLR 2024)
finding: A cascade where GPT-3.5-turbo answers first and its answer consistency decides whether to escalate to GPT-4 matches GPT-4 accuracy at 40% of the cost on six reasoning sets.
numbers: Average accuracy 0.929 (MoT cascade variants) vs 0.931 (GPT-4 CoT with self-consistency) at 40% of the cost. On CREPE 0.885 vs 0.871 at 47% of the cost.
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5/GPT-4), six reasoning benchmarks, prices at that time.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a second team finds the stop-at-sufficient shape pays on reasoning (60% cost cut at similar accuracy), smaller than FrugalGPT's 98% headline and still 2023 models.

source: Kotte (2026) UCCI: calibrated uncertainty for cost-optimal LLM cascade routing
finding: Isotonic calibration of token-margin uncertainty lets a cascade pick its escalation threshold from data. On a production NER workload it cut inference cost at fixed accuracy.
numbers: 75,000 queries, 4B and 12B instruction-tuned models. Cost -31% (95% CI [27%, 35%]) at micro-F1 0.91. ECE 0.12 to 0.03.
limits: Single-author preprint; one NER workload; small open models; not the 2025-2026 frontier price list.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a 2026 test finds a real but moderate saving (31%), well below FrugalGPT's best case. Calibrating the stop signal matters.

source: Search log, this run: arXiv API queries combining take-the-best, fast-and-frugal, recognition heuristic, ecological rationality, one-reason decision, fast-and-frugal trees with LLM / language models
finding: No paper was returned that prompts an LLM with take-the-best, a recognition rule or a fast-and-frugal tree and measures accuracy at equal tokens. Only Bogdan 2026 (arXiv 2606.15877) and the two ecological-prior papers (2402.01821, 2509.00116) appeared. One WebSearch returned the same plus an unrelated 2017 time-pressure paper; the session web-search quota then ran out.
numbers: About 12 arXiv queries on the topic; zero direct hits.
limits: Absence in two search tools is weak evidence. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited. Papers using other words (lexicographic prompt, sequential checklist) could have been missed.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6 stay open: the key experiment has not been published as far as these tools can show.
